title: Abraham believed (Romans 4)
hook: Abraham trusted God and it was counted as righteousness

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was but now, nuni de, the hinge of Romans. Your line was the story keeps going.

An old man stands outside his tent at night. He's well past seventy-five. His wife Sarah is old too, long past childbearing. They have no children, and by every sensible measure never will. And God takes him outside and says: look up, count the stars if you can. So shall your descendants be. Centuries later, in the middle of his big argument about grace, Paul needs one example everyone in Rome respects, Jew and Gentile alike. He doesn't pick a king or a prophet. He goes back to that old man under the stars.
screen: `AN OLD MAN UNDER THE STARS.` → `COUNT THEM, IF YOU CAN.` → `PAUL GOES BACK TO ABRAHAM.`

segments.voice: Paul quotes Genesis, in the King James Bible: "Abraham believed God, and it was counted unto him for righteousness." Believed: the Greek verb shares a root with pistis, faith, and means trust more than opinion. Abraham didn't agree to a list of ideas; he leaned his whole weight on a promise. Counted is an accountant's word in Greek: credited, entered in the ledger as being in the right with God. Timing matters too. In Genesis, this verse comes before Abraham is circumcised, before the covenant sign. So, Paul says, Abraham is the father of everyone who trusts like this: his own people, and the nations too. Abraham looked honestly at his own body, as good as dead at about a hundred, and at Sarah's, and still trusted. "Who against hope believed in hope." Genesis is honest too: Abraham and Sarah both laugh at the promise at different moments, and they try a plan of their own along the way. Faith here is not the absence of doubt. It's trusting anyway. Christians read this chapter alongside the letter of James, which also points to Abraham and says faith without works is dead. How the two fit has been argued over, sharply at the Reformation. Many Protestants today hear them as two sides of one coin; Catholic and Orthodox teaching stresses that faith and works belong together. Jews and Muslims also honor Abraham as a father of faith. After a week of big words, grace, sin, but now, it comes down to one old man, looking up, trusting.
screen: `PISTIS: TRUST, NOT OPINION.` · `COUNTED: CREDITED TO HIS ACCOUNT.` · `BEFORE THE SIGN, FATHER OF ALL.` · `AGAINST HOPE, BELIEVED IN HOPE.` · then, large: `ABRAHAM BELIEVED GOD.`

segments.voice: Think of one thing you're gripping tightly right now, a test result, a child far away, money, a decision you keep replaying, and hold it in your mind like something in your fist. Look at it honestly, the way Abraham looked at his own old body, then slowly open your hand. If you pray, hand that one thing to God and leave it there; if you don't, simply loosen your grip for two minutes and notice what happens in your chest.
Faith. Pistis in Greek: trust, leaning your weight on a promise. Abraham's was counted to him as righteousness.
Your line: counted as right. Trust, not proof, went into Abraham's ledger. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Christians often point to Abraham as the model of faith, and many pray by naming a specific worry and entrusting it to God, sometimes with the words of a psalm.

original.note: Greek: faith, trust, faithfulness. the same word can mean trusting and being trustworthy.

trapdoor: what you thought: faith means believing something without evidence.
what it means: Abraham trusted a promise while looking his situation in the face, and it was counted to him as righteousness.
what a scholar hears: elogisthē, counted, is bookkeeping language, and Paul's point about timing rests on Genesis 15 coming before the circumcision of Genesis 17.

notes: Ages: Abraham 'about an hundred years old' (Romans 4:19); Sarah ninety (Genesis 17:17). Script says 'about ninety' for Sarah and 'close to a hundred' in the hook; confirm.
The star-counting scene (Genesis 15:5) is placed at night outside the tent; the text says God 'brought him forth abroad', confirm the tent detail is acceptable as scene-setting.
Paul and James on Abraham: the one-line summary of how Protestants, Catholics and Orthodox reconcile them should be checked for fairness.
Neighbor mention: Jews and Muslims also honor Abraham as a father of faith. Brief and non-comparative; confirm.
Week-end look-back is folded into the end of the teach (grace, sin, but now).

Audit (wider sample): the hook put Abraham 'close to a hundred' and Sarah 'about ninety' at the star scene of Genesis 15, but those ages belong to Genesis 17 (Abraham was 75 at 12:4 and 86 at Ishmael's birth, 16:16); hook and fork now say only that they were old. 'The Greek noun behind believed' corrected (it is the verb pisteuo). The Paul-and-James line no longer implies the churches simply agree; it notes the Reformation argument.
